slides: Open by naming the chapter's problem: orientation is not a decorative arrow on a picture, but a sign choice that must survive changes of basis, charts, and loops. Use the dependency map as the route for the lecture. The left side starts with determinant signs in a single tangent space; the center turns those choices into manifolds through forms and charts; the right side shows where topology can obstruct a global choice.

Start in a vector space because nothing topological is hiding yet. Two ordered bases are equivalent exactly when the transition determinant is positive, so the artifact's four bases split into two positive and two negative classes. Ask students to predict the sign before reading the label: shears preserve handedness, reflections and swaps reverse it. This is the sign test every later construction localizes to tangent spaces.

Now replace an ordered basis by a nonzero top-degree alternating form. The form is positive on exactly one of the two basis classes, so it selects an orientation without needing a preferred basis. Emphasize that on a manifold this must be done smoothly and nowhere vanish. This slide is the conceptual bridge between linear algebra and the practical coordinate formula for orientation forms.

Move from one tangent space to a family of charts. An oriented atlas is a local sign system whose transition Jacobians are always positive on overlaps. Use the bar chart as a quick diagnostic: identity and positive shear glue, reflection and coordinate swap do not. The point is not the special examples; it is that every overlap carries a determinant sign, and one negative overlap in a loop can destroy a global orientation.

Collect the equivalent encodings before adding new constructions. A manifold orientation may be described by compatible tangent-space orientations, a positive atlas, or a nonvanishing top form. Products and pullbacks are then sign conventions applied to these encodings: products order factors, and local diffeomorphisms preserve orientation when the relevant determinant sign is positive. This is a vocabulary consolidation slide.

Boundary orientation is where ordering mistakes become visible. The notebook uses the outward-normal-first rule: put the outward normal first, then choose the boundary tangent so the ordered pair is positive in the ambient orientation. On the disk this forces the counterclockwise boundary direction, and the check records determinant one at all sampled angles. Mention hypersurfaces as the same normal-plus-tangent bookkeeping in one codimension.

Add a metric without losing the orientation distinction. The metric contributes a positive coefficient sqrt(det g), while the orientation decides whether that coefficient multiplies the chosen coordinate form or its negative. The heatmap is a density picture, not by itself an orientation picture. Stress the two-part statement: the determinant stays positive on the sample, and reversing orientation changes the sign of the volume form.

Use coverings to show why local orientation data may fail globally. The cylinder keeps each sheet of the orientation covering fixed after one loop, while the Mobius band swaps the positive and negative sheets. That single sign flip is the obstruction: there is no continuous global choice of one sheet. Connect this back to atlas signs by saying that transport around a loop multiplies the encountered signs.

Projective space is the compact test case for the same deck-transformation rule. The antipodal map on the sphere preserves the recorded orientation sign exactly for odd-dimensional real projective spaces in the table, so those entries are orientable. Then use the learner lab as an active check: an odd number of reflection overlaps gives total sign minus one and fails to glue, while an even number returns plus one.

Close with the sign audit students should carry forward. Every orientation question asks where the sign lives, how it changes under the allowed maps, and whether the choices glue around loops and boundaries. Tie each audit item to a slide artifact: determinant bases, atlas transitions, top forms, boundary normals, Riemannian volume, covering transport, and projective-space signs. End by warning that pictures help only after the sign convention is explicit.
